title: Fierce compassion
hookLine: compassion can say no, and act against harm

lines: THE OTHER EDGE OF THE BLADE.
cards: On a playground, one kid has another backed against the fence, and the smaller one is close to tears. A parent walks over. Not smiling.
Not yelling either. Just a level voice, a hand raised, and one word: "Stop." Then she stands between them until it's done.
Nobody watching would call that soft. And yet it's hard to call it anything but care. These compassion days have leaned gentle: warmth, gratitude, a kind inner voice.
Today is the other edge of the same blade.

teach.b: First, what compassion is for. Paul Gilbert, whose work on the inner critic came up earlier this week, describes compassion as being sensitive to suffering, together with a commitment to relieve and prevent it.
Prevent is an active word. Sometimes preventing harm means stepping in, saying no, or refusing to go along. Second, two sides.

The psychologist Kristin Neff, known for her research on self-compassion, writes about tender and fierce sides of it. The tender side comforts and accepts. The fierce side protects, sets boundaries and takes action.
In her account, both come from the same care; the fierce side is what that care looks like when something needs to change. Third, an old picture.
In Tibetan Buddhist art, some figures who stand for awakened qualities are painted with fierce faces, flames and weapons.
Teachers in that tradition explain the fierceness as compassion's strength, turned against harm and ignorance, not against beings. Fourth, a command to speak up.
In the book of Proverbs, a king's mother tells him what his position is for.
In the King James words: "Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy." Not just feel for them. Open thy mouth.
Fierce compassion isn't anger let off the leash. It keeps its eyes on the person being protected, and even on the person doing harm, who needs stopping too.

how: Some self-compassion programs teach both a tender side (comfort, acceptance) and a fierce side (protection, boundaries, action), and some religious traditions picture compassion with fierce as well as gentle faces.

o: care that protects and says no, without losing warmth
kindness so intense it overwhelms the giver
anger at wrongdoers, let loose for a good cause

p: plead the cause of the poor

s: compassion always means being soft and agreeable
Gilbert's definition includes preventing suffering, and Neff describes a fierce side that protects.
in Tibetan Buddhist art, some figures standing for awakened qualities have fierce faces
teachers in that tradition explain it as compassion's strength turned against harm.
fierce compassion is anger let off the leash
it keeps its eyes on the person being protected, and even on the one doing harm.

games.q: at work, a group keeps making jokes at a quiet coworker's expense. what does fierce compassion do?
o: laugh along so things stay friendly.
say, calmly, "that's enough," and check on the coworker later.
shout at the group until they're embarrassed.
games.why: fierce compassion steps in firmly to protect, without turning the moment into an attack.

practice: Sit tall, feet on the ground, and bring to mind someone who might need protecting, a child, a coworker, an older relative, or yourself, letting your back straighten as if you stood between them and harm: not tense, not angry, just steady.
If you like, find the one plain sentence you would say, "Stop," "No," "Not like this," and hold the steadiness with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Fierce compassion. Care that protects, says no and acts against harm, without losing its warmth. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: fierce and kind. Saying no can be its own kind of care. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Paul Gilbert, definition of compassion in his work on compassion-focused therapy
